lead: A heat engine sits between a hot body and a cold body. It takes heat Q₁ from the hot body, turns part of it into work W, and dumps the rest Q₂ into the cold body. Run the same device backwards and it becomes a refrigerator or a heat pump: now you pay work to carry heat from cold to hot. This is the machine behind every power plant, every air conditioner on a Chennai wall and every cold storage. This chapter fixes the vocabulary and the energy accounting for all of them. The second-law limit on how good they can be comes later in the unit.
prereq: You need: heat and work with their sign convention, and the first law applied to a cycle.

sections.h3: Source, sink and a cyclic device

blocks.text: A thermal reservoir is a body so large that adding or removing heat does not change its temperature. A lake, the atmosphere and a large furnace are treated as reservoirs in problems. The hot reservoir at T₁ is the source. The cold reservoir at T₂ is the sink. Temperatures are in kelvin, and T₁ is greater than T₂.

Every device in this chapter has the same three parts: a source, a sink, and a device placed between them. The device works in cycles, so it returns to its own state at the end of each cycle. Its internal energy therefore returns to the same value, and the net change over one cycle is zero. The first law for a cycle then connects only the heat and the work crossing the boundary.

blocks.where: Q₁ is the heat taken from the source, in kJ; W is the net work delivered by the device, in kJ; Q₂ is the heat given to the sink, in kJ. Heat into the device is positive and work done by the device is positive, the usual sign convention.

blocks.text: The same balance serves engines and reversed devices. Only the direction of the arrows changes, and with it which quantity you pay for and which one you want. That is why one chapter covers power plants, room air conditioners and hot-water heat pumps together.

A heat engine takes heat Q₁ from the source, converts part of it into work W, and rejects the rest Q₂ to the sink. The working fluid may be steam, air or burnt gas. The accounting is the same in every case.
η = W / Q₁ = (Q₁ − Q₂) / Q₁ = 1 − Q₂ / Q₁
blocks.where: η (Greek eta) is the thermal efficiency, a pure fraction; multiply by 100 for per cent. W is the net work output in kJ, Q₁ the heat supplied from the source in kJ, and Q₂ the heat rejected to the sink in kJ.

blocks.text: Efficiency is what you get divided by what you paid for. In an engine the payment is the heat Q₁ drawn from the source, so η is always less than 1 whenever Q₂ is greater than zero. A claim of 100% efficiency means Q₂ = 0, an engine that dumps no heat at all. That machine is forbidden by the second law, and the Kelvin-Planck statement states the ban precisely.
Watch the denominator. It is Q₁, not Q₂. Dividing work by the rejected heat measures nothing useful.

sections.h3: Running it backwards: refrigerator and heat pump

blocks.text: Reverse every arrow. Work W now goes in, heat Q₂ is pulled out of the cold space, and Q₁ = Q₂ + W is pushed into the warm room. The hardware is the same. What changes is which heat you want: the cold-side heat for a refrigerator, the hot-side heat for a heat pump.

COPR = Q₂ / W and COPHP = Q₁ / W
COP is the coefficient of performance, a pure number. Q₂ is the heat removed from the cold space in kJ, Q₁ the heat delivered to the warm space in kJ, and W the work input in kJ. Some syllabi call the COP the performance factor.
Divide Q₁ = Q₂ + W by W and you get COPHP = COPR + 1. A device with COPR = 1.667 becomes a heat pump of COP 2.667 on the same work.

A COP above 1 surprises students. It is not free energy. The COP compares heat moved with work paid, not heat with heat. Most of the heat moved was already sitting in the cold space and was only carried uphill. Energy in still equals energy out.

Room air conditioners are sold in tons of cooling. One ton of refrigeration is 3.517 kW of heat removed, so a 1.5 ton split unit removes 1.5 × 3.517 ≈ 5.3 kW of heat. If its compressor draws 1.5 kW of electricity, its COP is 5.3 / 1.5 ≈ 3.5.

spec.aria: Two energy-flow diagrams. A heat engine between 600 K and 300 K: 800 kJ in, 300 kJ of work out, 500 kJ rejected, efficiency 0.375. A refrigerator between a 270 K cold store and a 300 K room: 500 kJ taken from the store, 300 kJ of work in, 800 kJ to the room, COP 1.67 as a refrigerator and 2.67 as a heat pump.

examples.question: A cyclic engine receives 800 kJ of heat from a reservoir at 600 K and rejects 500 kJ to a reservoir at 300 K. (a) Find the work output and the thermal efficiency. (b) A refrigerator is driven by 300 kJ of work and removes 500 kJ of heat from a cold store at 270 K; the room around it is at 300 K. Find the heat it rejects to the room, its COP as a refrigerator, and its COP if used as a heat pump. Compare with the reversible limit T₂/(T₁ − T₂).
steps: (a) Work output from the cycle energy balance: W = Q₁ − Q₂ = 800 kJ − 500 kJ = 300 kJ.
Thermal efficiency: η = W / Q₁ = 300 kJ / 800 kJ = 0.375, that is 37.5%.
The reservoir temperatures are not needed for η; they set only the reversible limit 1 − 300/600 = 0.5 (see the Carnot cycle).
(b) Energy balance for the refrigerator cycle: Q₁ = Q₂ + W = 500 kJ + 300 kJ = 800 kJ rejected to the room.
COP as a refrigerator: COP<sub>R</sub> = Q₂ / W = 500 kJ / 300 kJ = 1.667.
COP as a heat pump (the wanted heat is now Q₁): COP<sub>HP</sub> = Q₁ / W = 800 kJ / 300 kJ = 2.667. Check: COP<sub>R</sub> + 1 = 1.667 + 1 = 2.667.
Reversible limit: 270 / (300 − 270) = 9. The actual 1.667 is far below it: allowed, but a poor, irreversible machine.
examples.answer: (a) W = 300 kJ and η = 37.5%. (b) 800 kJ is rejected to the room; COP<sub>R</sub> = 1.667 and COP<sub>HP</sub> = 2.667, well below the reversible refrigerator limit of 9 between 270 K and 300 K.

traps: Efficiency with the wrong denominator. η = W/Q₁, the heat taken from the source. Writing W/Q₂ gives 0.6 in the worked example, which means nothing.
Forgetting COP<sub>HP</sub> = COP<sub>R</sub> + 1, and quoting the same COP for a fridge and for a heat pump built on the same cycle.
Reading a COP of 3 as an efficiency of 300% or as free energy. The COP counts heat moved, not heat created; Q₁ = Q₂ + W still holds.
Confusing a ton of refrigeration with electrical power. One ton is 3.517 kW of heat removed; a 1.5 ton unit removes about 5.3 kW of heat but draws far less than that from the socket.

Feeding the reservoir temperatures into 1 − T₂/T₁ here. That formula belongs to a reversible engine; it gives 0.5 for the 600 K and 300 K reservoirs while the actual engine in the example gives 0.375.

quiz.q: Define a thermal reservoir and say why its temperature stays constant.
quiz.a: A body so large that any heat added or removed changes its temperature negligibly. The heat exchanged is small compared with its heat capacity, so its temperature is treated as constant.

quiz.q: Write the first-law energy balance for a heat engine cycle and define each symbol.
quiz.a: Q₁ = W + Q₂, where Q₁ is the heat from the source in kJ, W the net work output in kJ and Q₂ the heat rejected to the sink in kJ.

quiz.q: Why is a heat pump's COP always exactly one more than the refrigerator COP of the same device?
quiz.a: The heat pump delivers Q₁ = Q₂ + W to the warm space, while the refrigerator removes only Q₂ from the cold space, both for the same work W. Dividing by W gives COP<sub>HP</sub> = COP<sub>R</sub> + 1.

quiz.q: An engine takes 1200 kJ from a source and rejects 750 kJ to a sink. Find the work output and the thermal efficiency.
A refrigerator of COP 4 removes 8 kW of heat from a cold room. Find the work input and the heat rejected to the room.
quiz.a: W = Q₂/COP<sub>R</sub> = 8/4 = 2 kW; Q₁ = Q₂ + W = 8 + 2 = 10 kW rejected to the room.

quiz.q: A student claims an engine takes 1000 kJ from a source, delivers 400 kJ of work and rejects 700 kJ. Identify the error.
quiz.a: The first law fails: Q₁ − W = 1000 − 400 = 600 kJ, which should equal the rejected heat, but 700 kJ is claimed. Energy is not conserved, so no such engine can exist even before the second law is applied.

quiz.q: A 1.5 ton room air conditioner has a COP of 3.2. Find the heat it removes in kW and the electrical power it draws. Explain why the two differ.
quiz.a: Q₂ = 1.5 × 3.517 = 5.28 kW of heat removed. Power drawn W = Q₂/COP = 5.28/3.2 = 1.65 kW. All 5.28 kW of cooling is heat taken from the room, not made by the compressor. The 1.65 kW of electrical work is added to it, so the unit throws 5.28 + 1.65 = 6.93 kW to the outside air. The ton rating states cooling delivered, not electricity consumed.

beyond: Not for the exam. Manufacturers quote seasonal figures rather than a single COP: room air conditioners sold in India carry an ISEER star rating measured across a year of varying outdoor temperatures, and inverter compressors are scored at part load. Heat pump water heaters and heat pump dryers are growing markets because they deliver several kilowatts of heat per kilowatt of electricity. Data-centre cooling, electric-vehicle cabin cooling and district heating all rest on this same balance sheet. The vapour compression refrigeration cycle, met later in this subject, is the hardware behind these devices; search for ISEER, seasonal COP and heat pump water heater next.
